title: Tokyo Court Protects Human Voices in AI Clone Case
paragraphs: As artificial intelligence makes it easier to copy people's voices, a court in Japan has ruled for the first time that a person's voice can be protected by law.

The case was brought by Kenjiro Tsuda, a Japanese voice actor who is best known for playing the character Kento Nanami in the popular anime series "Jujutsu Kaisen." Tsuda is known for his deep voice. He took legal action against the anonymous operator of a TikTok account called "Nanami." The account had used an AI-generated copy of Tsuda's voice to narrate more than 180 videos about urban legends and paranormal events. By November 2025, the account had more than 200,000 followers, and many viewers commented on how similar the voice sounded to Tsuda's.

Tsuda argued that the account's operator had unfairly profited by using his voice to attract viewers, and he asked for the videos to be deleted. However, the operator argued that the voice had been created by AI, so it was not actually Tsuda's voice, and that the videos had not damaged his reputation.

At the end of September 2026, the Tokyo District Court issued its ruling. Presiding Judge Aya Takahashi stated that the human voice is symbolic of individual personality, just like a person's portrait. The court ruled that using someone's voice with a clear intention of exploiting its commercial appeal can violate their "publicity rights," which protect people's names and images from being used commercially without permission. According to reports, it was the first time a Japanese court had recognized such a right to one's voice.

However, Tsuda's request to have the videos deleted was rejected, because the account had already been closed. As a result, the court did not decide whether these particular videos had actually violated his rights. Tsuda's lawyer said that both sides could claim victory. TikTok said it would respect the decision.

Voice actors have become increasingly concerned about AI copies of their voices appearing on social media. The issue has also attracted attention elsewhere. In 2024, for example, OpenAI stopped using one of its ChatGPT voices after the actress Scarlett Johansson said it sounded eerily similar to her own.
